utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. Yes, I can follow in a language I understand, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances, Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic, and I just want to point out for the record that Mr. Cunningham and I continue to appear in the absence of a licence from the treasury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to this I did receive a communication which I cannot consider official because I received it through friends that I have in Washington, which confirms exactly what you said yesterday. Supposedly you should have received it by now but anyway -- but I feel I would not be exposing you or Mr. Cunningham to any risk if we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's our current feeling, Your Honour, based upon that permission document that was sent to Judge Meron but it really doesn't -- it's not a licence and that's the thing that concerns me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But for -- to be on the safe side, Madam Registrar, I would like you to extract this part of the transcript of today, as well as the first part of the transcript of yesterday, where Mr. Ackerman made a statement on the situation, as he considered it to obtain yesterday, and communicate both to the -- to Judge Meron, President Meron, for his information. Any preliminaries? Ms. Korner? Nothing? I have a very short matter to bring up with you, and I need your cooperation. On the 28th of April of this year, the Prosecution filed a motion, Rule 92 bis motion, relating to the admission of evidence under that rule relating to destruction of religious sites. You had responded, Mr. Ackerman, not objecting to the admission of these statements, but you did object to the admission of the attachments accompanying the statement of Witness 7.243. Now, the attachments consist of the following: One attachment is a kind of a brochure, a kind of a brochure in English, which I personally need to discuss with my two judges. I have not discussed it as yet, but which doesn't seem to be that much relevant but I'm open to conviction. The problem is the CD. This CD, having gone through it, there are two books in English. I would imagine that there are relevant parts of these two books and parts which are absolutely not relevant. I don't know. So if you already have a clue as to what is relevant and what is not, please let us know because that would put us in a better position at least to decide whether they should be admitted or not. Then there is another problem. There is another book in B/C/S which Mr. Ackerman hasn't objected to being admitted in evidence, but the thing is how can we decide to admit it in evidence if it is not translated in English so if it's not translated in English we are going to have a problem. We will probably admit it because there is no objection on the part of Mr. Ackerman, but what use we would be able to put to it frankly I don't know. So this is -- I'm just saying it -- also incidentally, you do not as such specify which attachments you object to, and I take it therefore that you are objecting to all attachments, all right? If I am wrong there, correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Ms. Korner, if you can take that up and help us please, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I regret to say that I can't. This is what is colloquially described as Ms. Richterova's baby and Ms. Richterova is not here today but she'll be back tomorrow and I'll make inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that and I thank you, Ms. Korner. Usher, please, the solemn declaration. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. We will proceed with your cross-examination and hopefully finish with you today. May I ask you, please, to repeat your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, take a chair and let's proceed. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We got off to a kind of shaky start yesterday with all of the mixup over documents and things and I'm hoping we can move rather rapidly now today based upon the agreement we have entered into regarding the use of these documents because I would like to finish with you today so that you can go back home. So if you'll cooperate with me I'll cooperate with you in that regard. I want to go just very briefly --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope so too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go very briefly to your testimony from yesterday. There was that portion of your testimony where you talked about the four horsemen of the apocalypse and named Mr. Brdjanin as one of those and in your statement of 24 November, 2001, on page 3, you claim that those four persons, Vukic, Kupresanin, Radic and Brdjanin, were responsible for what happened, and the question I have in that regard is this: With regard to Mr. Brdjanin, can you give us the name of any person you spoke to and the date upon which you approximately might have spoken to them, who told you that they had committed any kind of an offence, any kind of a crime, because of something they heard Mr. Brdjanin say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's rather ridiculous. Who would say that? Who can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. The interpretation that I got says that you used the word ridiculous. You cannot address anyone here with those adjectives.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I repeat to you, Mr. Ackerman here is doing his duty. And he has a right to be respected and allowed to do his duty. So there will not be a repetition of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I respect Mr. Ackerman and I am aware of what his role is here in this trial. Mr. Ackerman, nobody came and told me directly, you know, under the influence of Mr. Brdjanin I did so and so. Well, to expect something like that is not on. These people are not going to say what they have been doing. Nobody came up to me to say, this person provoked me to do such and such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you know. I'll ask you if you know, that a number of people who have been indicted by this Tribunal have in fact admitted that they've committed certain offences, they've pleaded guilty. They have done things like that. So that happens, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, my next question to you is this: I take it that you do not claim that these things that you've described that happened would not have happened if Mr. Brdjanin had not been there. You don't make that claim, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure how he can answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How can you speculate --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, my apologies to you for not having turned the microphone on. Objection sustained. You either rephrase your question, Mr. Ackerman, or put another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You claim, sir, that Mr. Brdjanin, among these four people, was responsible for what happened. I take it that the other side of that, you can't claim, that these things would not have happened but for the presence of Mr. Brdjanin. You can't make that claim, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only due to his presence, I don't think so, but he's one of the people who contributed to what had happened. Unfortunately this happened. Yes, you cannot just say that it is just Mr. Brdjanin who was creating the atmosphere and raising the tension, which would then result in the misfortunate that occurred but the fact is that he is one of them, that is certain, and there is no doubt about that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We are going to talk more about that as we get a little further on here with regard to certain things you said in your diary. I want to go back to your diary now and I'm going to the 15th of April, page L0034690. On that page, sir, you're quoting or referring at least to, and I think quoting, an article from Glas, and that article talks about the new insignia for the police, the Ministry of Interior insignia, and the oaths of loyalty that police officers were asked to take. The article indicates that in the Banja Luka Public Security Station, almost all Serbs have signed the oath of loyalty while the percentage of Muslims who followed suit was around 60 and for Croats that number was over 60. Do you recall recording that in your diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's -- that was copied from Glas. I remember copying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm now going to go to page -- it's actually the date of 16 April, 1992, page L0054895. And you -- you speak of an interview done by the Serbian Minister of External Affairs with an Iranian newspaper agency, and what you say that that Serbian Minister of External Affairs stated -- INTERPRETER: Microphone, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I am not receiving -- it's okay, it's okay. I thought there was something wrong but I'm receiving -- must have been some kind of disconnection here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you say in your diary is that Serbian Minister of External Affairs, Slobodan Jovanovic stated Muslims in the so-called third Yugoslavia will not be recognised as a people or nationality, but only as a religious community. Do you have any idea what he's talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, what you quoted to me a moment ago, and what you quoted just now as said by this Serbian minister, this was directly taken out either I typed out, copied the newspaper article so it wasn't my guessing. And this other thing, as far as I can see, is the interview that I've transcribed from the radio so what he's talking about -- well, he's talking about what Muslims were always talking about, it wasn't a nationality. It was an ethnic community. It was a religious community. It was the Serbs who became Islamisised. That's what -- the term that was used and this is what they have been talking about from the start.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know when it was in the history of Yugoslavia that the Muslim community of Yugoslavia was first recognised as a nationality? Given national status? Do you know when that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know that very well. I wasn't following that but I know that it happened during Tito's era.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go now to 17 April of 1992, and I'm on page L0065794. And just very briefly, you simply state there and I'm not sure we can tell where you got the information from, you simply state: "The Krajina economy is operating only at 40 per cent of its capacity."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, all of this data I found in the newspapers. I as a layman who was not part of it, I couldn't have made this up. All of this data is based on what I have read in Banja Luka press or heard from electronic media that were active in Banja Luka. It was not a secret. Everybody knew this in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, please understand. Because you're spending a lot of time defending yourself from accusations I'm not making. I'm not suggesting you made this up. I know you got it from some source, newspaper, magazine or something like that. I only want to point out --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Read, I read and copied, typed it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I simply want to point out that from some source you learned that the economy was operating at 40 per cent of its capacity. I'm not accusing you of making that up, okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that you're accusing me. I'm just explaining how I came by that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please be assured that if I take the position that you're making something up, I'll be very direct about that and tell you that that's how I feel, okay? I'm now going to 21 April of 1992 and the page is L0057081 in English and it's just -- this is just a very brief thing. You're speaking of the deterioration of Radio Banja Luka. You're commenting on a conversation that you heard on the radio, you're commenting on the deterioration of Radio Banja Luka and then you make -- you say this, and this is April of 1992: "But amazingly enough its music programme is replete with many melodies performed by Croatian artists." And that's an observation you made yourself just by listening to the radio, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see this here but I believe you if you have read it out, if I have written it, then that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd be happy to help you find it if you would like me to. It's right near the end of your diary for that day. It's under a quote from Goga. Goga says: "We would like to thank Nenad Stevandic, this concludes our conversation."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goga Stegic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then right under that, it's the last part of the interview that you're talking about. Right under that, at least in the English, there is a line and then you talk about this conversation is a mild illustration. It's the last paragraph -- it's the paragraph right before the last paragraph on that date, I think.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we don't have to waste time. I believe you. I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's more than believing me, you personally observed, you personally heard, that the music programme was replete with many melodies performed by Croatian artists. You knew that of your own knowledge, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, that happened until the appearance of the Serbian Defence Forces. After that, we did not know what we were listening to. We practically moved to Serbia. Instead of listening to songs about Vrbas Regura and so on we were listening about the Ibar River, Drina River, Morava River. This is what our children were learning in school. That's the truth, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, just a minute. Just a minute. On 21 April, that's what we were just talking about, was 21 April, on 21 April, you said: "Amazingly enough its music programme is replete with many melodies performed by Croatian artists." Now you say that was true until the SOS but the SOS arrived on the 3rd of April, and you're talking about the 27th; right? Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, but that's why I've written it down that it was a surprising thing. Something happened and on that day, that's what was broadcast, many Croatian singers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 27 April is where I'm going now. L0055314.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And so is everybody else, I gather. I'm not the only one. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I am receiving you in English now or at least I heard the word "testing". Can you say something else, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can hear you so I take it that we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We were getting ready to talk, sir, about page L0055314. And this is 27 April of 1992, and there you're writing about an announcement from the BH Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, that the JNA should withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then you say it was announced that members of the army could join the newly established TO forces and they were called upon to put themselves at the disposal of the legal organs of authority of this republic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand the question. Could you please repeat it for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. On that date, on 27 April, at the particular page of the diary that I'm referring to, you're talking about President Alija Izetbegovic announcing that the JNA should withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then you record this: "It was announced that members of the army could join the newly established TO forces and they were called upon to put themselves at the disposal of the legal organs of authority of this republic." And my question about that is: This was a call by Izetbegovic, I take it, to get the JNA members in Bosnia-Herzegovina to join up with the Muslim-Croatian TO to become part of what was later to become the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, this was no Muslim-Croatian TO. This Muslim-Croatian TO, how would you make General Siber, a Croat or Jovan Divljak, a Serb general, tie in with that. That's not what we are talking about here. That was different. This was a call on those young men to leave the army, the army, becoming ever-more aggressive, and to start defending their own home country, Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's how I understood the invitation that was issued to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it turned out then that the vast majority of people who became part of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were in fact Muslim with some notable exceptions like Jovan Divljak which was also true of the Army of Republika Srpska which had Muslim officers and Muslim soldiers serving in that army, so there was mixture in both armies, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a fact, isn't it, that when certain JNA forces tried to leave Sarajevo, that they were blocked by Muslim forces and not allowed to leave with their weapons? That happened, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know what you mean. You mean the -- when Kukanjac left, when he came out, yes, this did indeed happen. But if you remember, there was an agreement reached before the representative of the international forces, and this agreement said that the weapons were to be left behind as well as the documents, and that only the soldiers of the JNA were free to leave because the weapons, for God's sake, we were the ones who had paid for those weapons, not only the Serbs, not the Serbs alone. It was all of us who paid for that, the weapons. I really don't understand why Bosnia and Herzegovina should have less of a right to obtain something that Croatia and Serbia already had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm really not quarrelling that there is a lack of right. I'm just trying to make sure that the Chamber understands all of the facts about what was happening at that time. And I appreciate you helping me in that regard, I appreciate it a lot.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try hard, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know. And I appreciate it very much that you're doing that. I want to go now to 5 May of 1992. I don't know if you recall that but 5 May of 1992 was the date on which the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was formed. On that date, you refer to an interview on the radio with Mr. Brdjanin, and Mr. Brdjanin is being asked about the mobilisation, and you report and I assume correctly, that he said, mobilisation is being carried out in order to prevent war and to safeguard peace.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that this is correct. You can't lead this out in the future. I believe this is correct. As you can see, I also took down what your client said in terms of positive things, not merely the negative things. I wasn't only pointing out the negative things he said. I said what he -- I wrote down what he said. And he really did say this, but Mr. Ackerman, how can it happen, I am asking you now, that all the citizens somehow saw that this was not for the purpose of peace, of preserving peace? No one in Banja Luka had any illusions whatsoever that Mr. Brdjanin was some kind of a peace keeper or the dove of peace. That's what he called himself. But what was being talked about was one thing and it was what was being done was something entirely different. Unfortunately that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have been critical of Mr. Brdjanin for the things he said, and now you're telling us that he said a lot of things that had to do with peace and I want to show you another one, if you go to -- if we go over to page 03036115, Mr. Brdjanin was asked, "Will members of other nationalities" - talking about this mobilisation again - "Will members of other nationalities join the TO units, even minorities in the areas of Bosanska Krajina?" Mr. Brdjanin said, "Well, of course they will, of course. Even in the Partisans the first to come were Osman Karabegovic and the Maza brothers and so on. All those who want to live in these areas will join in. Of course I'm not saying that they will. Maybe they will not want to but those who are thinking rationally will join in and defend this place together." He said that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take your word for it, if that's how it was written down, then he said it. But this is all talk, empty talk. Who was there to defend from? Who? That's the only reply I'm looking for from you. Who was Banja Luka supposed to defend from in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The way things work here is I ask questions and you give answers. But it seems to me that when Mr. Brdjanin says something that you find offensive, then it's not just talk, but when he says something that's favourable then it's just talk but let me go on to the next one, 03036118 part of the same interview, Mr. Brdjanin says this: "All those who are contemplating leaving Bosanska Krajina, regardless of whether they are Serbs, Croats or Muslims will be sharply warned and other parts of Serbia and perhaps Montenegro will be told not to accept them. They should not be leaving these parts now when they are needed the most by their people. I'm allowing, and those in the crisis area to save their children," and so on. And again that's something you reported that Mr. Brdjanin said during this interview. That certainly doesn't sound like some policy to ethnically cleanse the area of Croats and Muslims but a policy to keep them from leaving, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I believe there is a misunderstanding between us here. No one said, and I never wrote down, well, it is there in my diary, I see your relying on my diary. Whatever Mr. Brdjanin said I wrote down. If he said something that could have been interpreted as meaning well, I did write that down too. I'm not accusing him but you needed to be there. You needed to be in the town to sense the atmosphere, to understand the atmosphere and everything that was going on and then if you had been there you would have understood what the words meant to people. Our life was completely normal, nothing much was happening, and they started telling us no one would be in your way, and emigrations, everyone joining the TO, everyone. You know why everyone? Everyone was free to leave but not everyone was joining because not everyone was allowed to join the TO. They were still acting the part of Partisans, the liberators. There was still this act being put on, we are the right people, and the Chetnik insignia were being concealed but those were later to shine in their full splendor and Biljana Plavsic was here was to go to Jazovac a place near Gradiska and she stated openly: "I'm proud to be in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Chetnik Jazovac." Please. They were pretending they were Partisans who would go there and liberate the Serbian people. Where? In Croatia. They were liberating Croatia from the Croats and Bosnia-Herzegovina was to be liberated from the Bosniaks. That was the final aim. This was just a brief introduction. This was putting in their measuring rod and seeing how the international community would react. Whenever there was a sharp reaction from the international community, they would immediately quiet down a little bit and watch for reactions from the international community. As soon as reactions were reserved, they would step up, step the whole thing up, and that was the truth of it. Unfortunately. Mr. Ackerman, if you believe that I'm a fortunate man to be sitting here now, giving you my testimony, which may cost your client dearly, you are far wrong. I would be far the happier man if the war had never happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if I'd never had to write this bloody diary. I can't even stand to look at it now. I would indeed have been very fortunate if none of this had ever come to pass. I wish I could just wake up one day and realise it was all just one bad nightmare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. Ms. Korner, yesterday -- let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I'm staying with the same radio interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because we are still in private session. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says open session here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'm now going to page 03036119 in the English. Mr. Brdjanin is asked if he has anything to add at the end, and he says this: "From the bottom of my heart and soul, I am appealing to the citizens of Bosanska Krajina to help out in safeguarding peace. Going to war does not benefit any people. No people in this world likes to wage war. That is why we are keeping the peace." Now presumably, this is a programme that's being broadcast fairly widely throughout the Krajina on Radio Banja Luka, and presumably being heard by a number of people; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. But on the same show, you can tell immediately, it's just that there is Bulic's statement claiming on the same show --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please, please. Only question I asked you was whether it was being broadcast widely across the Krajina. I didn't ask you about Bulic's statement. Okay? If you want to talk about it and be here tomorrow, I'll permit you to do that but I think you just sort of agreed that you'd like to go home today. So you make your own choice in that regard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what I should tell you. We are talking about Brdjanin, about his call on the people of Krajina, the call for peace, and on the same show, you have a man appearing who was the commander of some kind of security services centre saying that fires had been started -- that a barracks in Seba had burned down, that explosive devices had been thrown at the Lotus Cafe and many other explosions outside Banja Luka. In Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. peace time, prior to these unfortunate events, we didn't talk about peace. We lived peace. Peace was our life. Now, it is not my aim to challenge if Mr. Brdjanin indeed said some positive things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question -- let's go back to the question, sir. The question that was asked of you, I did allow you to speak because I still think that what you said was important, and fits in the question that Mr. Ackerman put to you. What Mr. Ackerman wants to know from you, whether such broadcasts were fairly widely transmitted throughout the Krajina on Radio Banja Luka, and presumably being heard by a number of people. Would you consider it in other words a voice in the wilderness or was it something that was broadcast on a regular basis, one would be able to follow it on a regular basis on Radio Banja Luka? Was this a common occurrence or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe I've already answered this. Yes. It was broadcast very widely across the Krajina and people did listen to it. Shows were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Stop there. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go now to 6 May of 1992, L0055644. Mr. Brdjanin is talking about -- I think this is from Glas but I'm not sure. It might be the radio. Mr. Brdjanin is talking about -- it's a press conference. Talking about decisions of the ARK war staff, said they must be implemented, and he says the first thing was that able-bodied men age 18 to 60 are forbidden to leave. Then on that same page, he says this: "We simply will not allow the flames of war to move to the very heart of Krajina, that is Banja Luka. Yes? On 10 May, 1992, L0054973, you talk about a war staff session of 9 May, 1992. It's not clear whether this comes from Glas or from the radio. Part of that that I'm interested in is the next page. You talk about the order it has to do with Atlas travel agency being band, Putnik travel agency not to sell tickets to men between 18 and 60, and so forth. Then you say that the order was signed by the chairman of the war staff, Radoslav Brdjanin. Now, I take it you really don't know if Brdjanin signed it. The indication that you had was that it was signed in his name but you don't know if Mr. Brdjanin himself actually signed it, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know what I heard over the radio. Now, whether that was correct or not, I really can't say. If something was published on the radio, a piece of information, my part was to write that down. Now, the radio people themselves may have misinterpreted something which is something I can't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know, have you learned, did you ever learn, that a large number of the documents issued by the ARK Crisis Staff were not signed by Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If that's asserted as a piece of evidence, it's not there. Are you asking him whether he knows? That's a different matter. But if it's asserted that they weren't signed by him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. You're perfectly right and I will restrict the question to what you have just indicated now. Are you in a position, sir, to answer that question from your own knowledge? First-hand information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult for me to say now how many of those had been issued -- those issued by the Crisis Staff were actually signed by Mr. Brdjanin. It's very difficult for me to say. I didn't really have -- well, yes, I had my informers, let me make this clear, informers close to him but you couldn't check every single document. What was really important is that he was at the very heart of the Crisis Staff, Radoslav Brdjanin was the key figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My God, how? As what? In what capacity? How would I agree to that? I was an ordinary citizen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- who was trying to keep a low profile.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You just told us that Mr. Brdjanin was at the heart of the Crisis Staff and a key figure, and then you admitted you never went to a Crisis Staff meeting. You have no idea what role he played in meetings of the Crisis Staff, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. You are misinterpreting my words. I didn't say I didn't have a clue. I did have a clue. I listened. Ninety per cent of the territory, of the area in terms of newspaper coverage, 50 per cent of the air time, given to the representatives of the Crisis Staff of the war staff. All this, all this was given over to Mr. Brdjanin as a leader. He was the spokesperson and the main man, and you can see that. You can see that from documents that the -- this Court has. You can also see from my unfortunate diary. It is well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really understand what you're saying but that doesn't go to my question. You have no idea inside Crisis Staff meetings what role if any Mr. Brdjanin played. You don't know if he was outvoted, and still had to issue the decisions, you don't know if he voted for or against them, you don't know any of that, do you? It's okay to say you don't know something if you don't, and I think you don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't expect him to have answered that question before, because that was not the question that you put to him, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're putting a completely different question forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, I don't quite know whether you have understood that you have to answer the question. It's being put to you that since you never attended any meeting of the Crisis Staff, you're not really in a position to tell us what was indeed the role that Mr. Brdjanin played in that -- in the course of the Crisis Staff meetings. In other words it's being suggested that if you were asked do you know if he was ever outvoted, you're not in a position to answer that, whether he had -- still had to issue a decision in spite of the fact that he wouldn't agree with it, it's being suggested to you that you're not in a position to answer that and so on and so forth. Are you in a position to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. It is certain that I don't know what has been happening and I can't say that I know or don't know that he had been outvoted. How can I say that I know? Of course not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going now to 13 May, 1992, sir. L0047474. You're reporting on -- when I say you're reporting, please understand that I'm always saying that you're reporting what was reported by this -- in this case Radio Banja Luka. You're reporting about a parade that was held on 12 May, 1992, of the CSB units in Banja Luka, and the newspaper there. The radio reported that this parade was attended by Nikola Koljevic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Branko Djeric, Radislav Vukic and Milan Martic but no indication that Mr. Brdjanin was there, is there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wasn't there. If it doesn't say so in the diary, then he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, for the record, according to what I have on my CD, at least, it's not what you asked the witness about does not show on 47474 but 47475.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In mine it's on 74. You may have a different translation than I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm always one step ahead, Mr. Ackerman. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've made that observation, Your Honour, more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 14 May, 1992, L0080674. You speak of a person by the name of Vida -- we better go to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this person you're referring to, Vida Husedzinovic, was a Serb --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Or is a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her real last name, I mean maiden name, I think, is Grandic, Vida Grandic, and she was married. She had been married, rather, to a journalist Husedzinovic, and that's where she has that last name. She had a son. I don't know his name. But I know that later on, he became Sasa, and in order to gain some privileges, she became the member of the Association of Serbian Sisterhood and a very regular member.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And she had something to do with the cultural centre. I mean, she's referred to here as the former and probably future director?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then what I see written here as -- is this: And we are now in May of 1992. The words I see in your diary are the following: "At the same time, at the cultural centre Vida Husedzinovic gets rid of two Serbs, Branko Sestic and Milan Stijak and employs two Croats and one Muslim."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, Vida was still playing to this effect. She didn't know how things would play out later. That same lady, Mrs. Husedzinovic gave me the keys to the Banski Dvori. I was allowed to let people go in there when I was making a tape, a videotape in Banja Luka. She thought at the time that everything that was going on in the name of the Serbs at risk, that she wanted to do the right thing, but then when she saw that this wouldn't happen, she then became the member of the Association of Serbian Sisterhood, got rid of those people from work, and then that's how she then turned her coat. They are all turncoats, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go now to 16 May of 1992, and the page I'm interested in is L0054850. And this comes from Glas and it talks about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- a report from the meeting of the Crisis Staff. It doesn't say whether Mr. Brdjanin was present at that meeting or took part in this decision. But the decision that it refers -- that I'm wanting to refer to was this: "Particularly severe measures shall be applied against those who misuse the uniform and insignia of the police, Territorial Defence and the army, and those who stop citizens to check their papers, control traffic, search flats or other facilities without a proper authorisation to do so." Now, that sounds like a measure designed to try to keep the peace and avoid some of the problems that were existing in the area at the time, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it sounds like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next day, and I'm now going to page -- it's 17 May, going to page L0072832, this is a comment by you: "Tomorrow is D-day, at least according to rumours around town. Panic and fear from 20th has already culminated in mass exodus of people of all ethnic denominations from this town."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to remind myself of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're right, it is the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the 19th, I'm sorry. Ms. Korner is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He doesn't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't have it there, sir, it's the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall what you meant when you said "Tomorrow is D-day"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, really. It's hard for me to recall. I would have to look at it for a while. I'd have to read through to see what was happening at the time. Then I would certainly be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says, "Panic and fear from the 20th has already culminated in a mass exodus of people of all ethnic denominations from this town." Does that jog your memory at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, if you had seen the diary and you have, you can see that a couple of days earlier, there was a showdown between the Serb police and the Serb defence forces where three members of the Serb defence forces were killed. The situation was such that people lived in fear. The curfew was introduced in Banja Luka so that looting could be allowed and I have proof of this. The police was distributing what's been looted, what's been looted, what the criminals have looted, people like Vedran Mandic and the others. The Serb defence forces, you're able to see that, they were threatening through the newspapers. The Serb defence forces were threatening because of the murder of Inspector Milorad Sufnica, and then they were threatening saying that if these people didn't hand themselves over within 48 hours, then they would be the ones who would get to them. They said it was a Muslim-Croatian conspiracy and all that. People found that very hard to swallow. Nobody could be protected. This commander of the police station, I've forgotten his name, he raped a couple of women. He brought them to the police station and raped them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have to stop you because we are -- you are going far, far beyond who was asked from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is a simple one. I appreciate -- that will be the end of the story. The question was, do you recall what you meant when you wrote in your diary, "Tomorrow is D-day"? I will read out to you the relevant part from your diary. "Tomorrow is D-day. At least, according to rumours around town. Panic and fear from 20th has already culminated in mass exodus of people of all ethnic denominations from this town. The town's first man, Predrag Radic, was invited to speak on the radio this morning to reassure the public." Now, having read out to you what you wrote in your own diary on the 19th of May of 1992, can you tell us what you meant by "D-day"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I can't recall, if I look through, then -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, if we go to the 22nd of May, L0080554, I'm interested in the first page there, and it's very -- it's a very simple question, I think: This -- your entry there indicates -- and it's being handed to you. Your entry there indicates that the executive council of ARK, headed by Nikola Erceg, was continuing to operate in parallel to the ARK Crisis Staff during this period of time, and in fact, on this date, 22 May of 1992, the Crisis Staff approved Erceg's proposal for a cabinet of the Autonomous Region of Krajina government. I think you can just answer that with a yes Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it appears from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what it says. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Under the system, the government system at that time, in Bosnia, former Yugoslavia, the executive council was the executive branch of the government and the assembly, the legislative branch of the government. That's true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These questions are not the ones I would like to answer, for the reason that I wrote down in my diary some daily events. I was not conducting any kind of policy. So please allow me not to answer. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all you had to say was you don't know and I wouldn't have insisted then. 25 May of 1992, L0072791. This appears to be some observations being made by you, and if we go down two-thirds of the way, almost three-quarters of the way down the page, you make this observation: "Also the word is out that the main hassle with mobilisation has passed since the army doesn't know what to do with so many people who signed up. They have no more uniforms or food to feed those people. Some say that the group currently training at Manjaca are virtually going hungry, have no arms at all (the group is of mixed ethnicity)." Do you recall writing that and where you might have learned that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wrote it down and found out about it from -- you see, people brought information, some information we received. At that time we were cheered by that. Later on, I think it was the 18th, when mobilisation happened, so it -- we got cheered up for nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On 26 May of 1992, at L0057040 - and I'm sure you'll remember this, I don't think you need to even look at it - you report in some detail the killing of Arkan. You recall that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The supposed killing that was broadcast on BHTV, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you refer to him as the leader of the Beli Orlovi, the White Eagles, in your report about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what it says in the diary, that is -- that's what I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know today that both those things you reported there were not true, that he wasn't killed and that he wasn't the leader of the White Eagles, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take them one by one, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: First of all, you know that he wasn't actually killed, what you reported there was not true.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You're right, Mr. Ackerman. Except that in -- further on in my diary, I corrected this. I only carried, or rather, reported, copied the information carried by the radio, so what they broadcast, that's how I wrote it down. Later on in the diary, I corrected this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we'll get there in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want him to answer the second part of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also know now that your report that he was the leader of the Beli Orlovi, the White Eagles, was also not true, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know -- I certainly know that he was the leader of the Tigers, but I'm telling you again, it is BH radio that carried this news and I just typed out what they broadcast. I said what the source was, and it's their mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm not suggesting it's your mistake, I'm just suggesting that you recorded it in your diary and you later learned it was not true. That's all. Nothing else. Okay. I want to go now to 27 May of 1992, L0054912. On that page, you talk about -- let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Are we -- yes. Sir, I'm going now to 2 July of 1992, the page is L0047559. It's very difficult to tell where this comes from since only a part apparently of your diary on that date has been translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We don't have that page for the witness because it wasn't one of the ones that we were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it got left off, Your Honour. I had someone else making the list because I didn't have time to do it myself, and ordinarily she is quite a competent individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please. Yes, which part are you going to refer the witness to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's right in the middle of the page beginning with the words, "the War Presidency."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The whole paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, please follow carefully what I am going to read out to you from your own -- from your own diary. The interpreters will be translating. In your war diary you wrote as follows: "The War Presidency will undertake stringent measures to evict all those who have broken into other people's flats. In addition to that, the breakers-in will be banned for at least three years from applying for a flat in the territory of the Banja Luka municipality, said Predrag Mitrakovic member of the War Presidency. Adding that the punitive measure is still in the form of a conclusion but the proposal will soon be on the agenda of a municipal assembly session."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I have several questions about that. First of all, there had been in existence for sometime a problem of persons breaking into empty flats and just moving into them and taking them over; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were many refugees in town, Serb refugees primarily, who had come to Banja Luka from Croatia and parts of Bosnia where they had basically been kicked out; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this passage that the Judge just read to you from your diary, it refers to the War Presidency and Predrag Mitrakovic. That would have been the Banja Luka War Presidency, would it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what it says was that the -- what the War Presidency did in this regard at the time was still in the form of a conclusion but that it would soon go to the municipal assembly so that it could be confirmed and then have the force of law; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who Mitrakovic was at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't really thinking about that. I merely recorded what he said. I know that he was a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On the next page, you recorded this: "Referring to the conflict of jurisdiction between AR Krajina and the municipal authorities, Mitrakovic underlined that all contentious issues must be resolved. We believe that we have jurisdiction over our municipality, although we do respect hierarchy. That is why we have suspended the decisions of the AR Krajina Crisis Staff in two cases only, said Mitrakovic." So what I take from that is that the Banja Luka municipality felt free to basically ignore the Crisis Staff when it was in their interest to do so. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you ever made aware that the Crisis Staff in Prijedor took an even stronger stance and totally refused to recognise any decision of the ARK Crisis Staff for a significant period of time? If you don't know that, that's fine. You may not have heard that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I now want to go to 7 July of 1992, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we haven't got that either. The list that was given to us this morning was a bit late so we didn't bring that. We only went on the basis of what you asked us for yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Ms. Korner. In fact, we have a problem too. We need a reference because it's telling us 7 July, Glas, is, you know, asking us to work miracles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we are still in private session, we can put it up on the ELMO, the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually we can put this page up on the ELMO anyhow, I've got the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there should be difficulties in putting on the ELMO an extract from a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not an extract from a newspaper. It's him quoting a newspaper again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ah, all right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think there is any difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I misunderstood the -- misread the list, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see, no. The English is on Your Honour's screen but the -- of course it's the witness who doesn't have the B/C/S so I can have my paper copy back, please. Do Your Honours have it up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, I think somebody will have to read it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me do that very quickly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, what this refers to is a news story from Glas dated 6 July, referring to some remarks made by Colonel Bogdan Subotic, Defence Minister of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to that, Subotic in fact was the Defence Minister of Republika Srpska at the time, I think. In any event, what Subotic said was: "On the occasion that the establishment of Crisis Staffs did not have a legal founding, and it was simply a case of copying something that the Ustasha created and introduced into Croatian practice." In other words, Subotic was saying that the Crisis Staffs were illegal and there was no basis for their having existed in the first place. I'm sure you remember that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember that very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because that was the beginning of what turned out to be quite a storm over whether or not Crisis Staffs were legal or illegal or appropriate, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And amazingly, if we go to 9 July, on page L0080309, even Nikola Erceg, chairman of the executive council, argues that we can do without a Crisis Staff when he was the person who had actually appointed it in the first place. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hardly. As if through a mist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You know, do you not, that at least by the 17th of July, of 1992, the Crisis Staff had ceased to exist? The ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look, for instance, at I think you allude to that and I'll have to ask you if that's what you intended. If you look at your diary for 19 July, skip ahead here for a bit, at L0081209, you say Radoslav Brdjanin, president of the, in parens, non-existing closed parenthesis, War Presidency of the AR Krajina and it talks about him appearing on television. But I think you are the one that put in the material in parentheses, the non-existing War Presidency of AR Krajina because of your understanding that it had ceased to exist by that point; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe you're right. If something is clearly marked as a quotation, and the quotation marks, what they are supposed to do at least in my opinion, is to put a question mark over what's being said, a written. This Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. So what you're saying is that it was the person who you were quoting that had referred to the Crisis Staff as non-existing? Which I can accept also. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I don't want us to go down a wrong track, so I'll point out to Mr. Ackerman that there are further entries showing that the War Presidency existed after that date, and Radoslav Brdjanin was in fact the President of the War Presidency. They changed the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think there is -- I'm not sure we are in agreement about that, Your Honour. Ms. Korner has said for the record in this case that the -- yeah --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's something that we will take up at a later stage, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that particular quote that you have in your diary on that date we have been referring to, that appearance by Brdjanin on television, what he did was announce his candidates for the new editor of Glas. He said he would like it to be either Dr. Savo Capljic or Nenad Novakovic, and the fact is that neither of the persons he wanted to be the new editor of Glas actually became editor; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. If he had announced them and they didn't become that, then that was supposedly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we are going to go back now to talk about what happened with regard to Glas just a little bit. If you look at -- I'll tell you, on 11 July of 1992, L0059139, it's an article from Glas dateline 10 July, reports that Kupresanin and Brdjanin held a press conference at which basically they announced that Miro Mladjenovic should be removed from his position as editor of Glas and you of course --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- are very familiar with that series of events. And as those events unfolded, Mladjenovic basically ignored Brdjanin and Kupresanin, he fought back against Brdjanin and Kupresanin, and said that he was not under their jurisdiction or control, and that only if the municipality, the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, called for his dismissal would he feel like he had to step down. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's true. It was a struggle for the control of the media. You have to know that Miro Mladjenovic was a man who was in favour of paramilitary formations, particularly of Miroslav Milinkovic and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the second name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what Kupresanin and Brdjanin didn't like, they needed to have more space in Glas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Miro Mladjenovic was very close, was he not to -- the name just left me, the leader of the Wolves of Vucjak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that. I said that. Veljko Milankovic, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Brdjanin of course had on several occasions criticised paramilitary formations and asked they be disbanded, and so that was part of the issue that was going on between them, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, the conflict started when Vojo Kupresanin stated that over 70 per cent of Serb soldiers were looting and thieving on the front, and I think that's why the misunderstanding occurred, which later on result in this struggle for the control of Glas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, after the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka met and actually dismissed the editor, I think it was your observation that even though he'd been -- Mladjenovic had been dismissed, that he continued to work behind the scenes and affect the editorial policies of the Glas newspaper. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think on 23 July of 1992, at page 00 -- L0056125, you referred to Glas as Miro's Glas and you said, "I'm saying Miro's Glas because he clearly continues to have a firm hold of all the strings, although he does not call himself editor-in-chief." Do you recall writing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, yes. I recall that, yes. Mladjenovic was at that time quite powerful. He had many followers at the time as well, and he was supported by Milankovic's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, do you recall a quote from Milankovic that if anybody gets rid of Mladjenovic, that they will die or something to that nature? Do you recall something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall him threatening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to take you to 16 July of 1992, and it's page L0058079. And we are back to this dispute that was going on about whether Crisis Staffs were legal or not. You're talking about the editor of desk, Goran Trkulja. You know who that is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trkulja, yes, yes, I do know. He was a journalist of Glas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You refer to something he wrote. You say this: "According to Goran Trkulja, the signatory Radoslav Brdjanin was aware that the institutions he represented could not pass decisions so he resorted to the good old communist methods, issued conclusions and referred them for decision to the deputies of the municipal assembly, the founder of the paper." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that. That was Trkulja's thinking so that was what Goran Trkulja was thinking, and I just copied that in my diary, I transferred it as interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's that same issue we talked about a moment ago, that a conclusion from a Crisis Staff does not have the force of law and must be referred and confirmed by an assembly. And I don't know if -- I think you told me that you really didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to answer that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to answer that question. Because it's not a question. It's a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On 17 July, sir, L0083019, there is reference again from Glas to this person we talked about yesterday, Nikodin Cavic from the Serbian Radical Party and you quote him in Glas as saying, "As for the Krajina War Presidency, their influence is not felt anywhere except in Banja Luka." Do you remember that story? Do you remember that entry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that announcement, Cavic, well, that was ridiculous what he said. It was just meant for the most naive ones, how -- what does he mean not having any influence? What he had was enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's probably referring to things like happened in -- we talked about in Prijedor, where they ignored what the Crisis Staff was doing and maybe even talking about in Banja Luka where he says they had influence, where they rejected decisions of the Crisis Staff. Don't you suppose that's what he's talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has already told you, Mr. Ackerman, that he knows nothing about the Prijedor matter or event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I withdraw the whole question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 28 July, sir and it's page L0046843. It's another article from Glas. It's about the agency for resettlement in Banja Luka and Glas reports according to you, which I'm sure is accurate, as follows: "The Banja Luka-based agency for resettlement of population and exchange of property --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, slow down when reading, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "-- for the AR Krajina, which was set up on 12 June, 1992, pursuant to the decision of the AR Krajina Crisis Staff, with the office in the former Mejdan 2 local commune, successfully resettles citizens of all three ethnical groups." Do you independently know that to be true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was true, yes. That was the truth. They successfully resettled us, yes, very successfully. You can see the consequences. (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we should redact this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we redact, please, lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, wait until we get into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm now going to 1 August of 1992. And this is what you are reporting here and the page I'm really interested in is L0081492. You are reporting a fairly extensive interview with Rajko Kasagic, a deputy in the SRBH assembly, and president of the Banja Luka municipal executive committee. And at one point on page 1492, they are talking about a meeting of the assembly, he's asked if Brdjanin was present at that meeting, and he says "No, he wasn't." He's then asked if the decisions of that assembly mean that Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies will be cancelled where legal civilian authorities can operate? His answer was this: "The assembly in fact only confirmed its earlier decisions about the operation of War Presidencies at the municipal level. Regions were not discussed at all because the Serbian republic BH constitution does not recognise them as such." In other words, what he's saying is that the constitution doesn't recognise regional organisations and therefore they didn't choose to even address whether regional Crisis Staffs were legal or illegal, since the whole concept of regionalisation was not constitutional or not part of the constitution. Isn't that the way you read that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I think it was completely taken out of context. You have to look at the whole interview to see how this applies. It starts off with a complaint at page L0081489 about the regions not passing on notices of this assembly. So you can't just take that completely out of context of the whole interview has to be looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the whole interview is in evidence. I agree with Ms. Korner that the whole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- should be looked at. I'm just dealing with one small part of it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we need to bring to the attention of the witness -- you didn't -- to the attention of the witness the rest of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's several --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The rest of the entry any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's several pages so I'm not going to do that because I don't have time to go through this entire interview. It's quite long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, the report says what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It does. It speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 3 August of 1992, the page I'm interested in is L0054140. And again, when it comes to Mr. Brdjanin, you are reporting a rumour and you say this: "As for Brdjanin, the rumour is getting louder here that he is finished or at least hanging by his nails. There are two stories on the city grapevine according to one he has resigned from his position in the autonomous province government, whereas according to the other, he has simply been removed. The truth remains to be seen." Do you recall writing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly. And stressed that this was hearsay, rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I read that it was. I think I was fair to you about that. Right after that, when we go to the next page --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You then start referring to articles from today's Glas, and in that context, you quote from an article and at page L0054142, the following language appears, which I believe to be simply your quote from Glas: "The regional government has asked for the status and position of the SRBH, and particularly the 1st Corps, to be defined, which is utterly unacceptable. At its last session, the assembly of the SRBH extended a formal recognition to the army for the tasks accomplished until then and set out clear guidelines for the future actions of the state government. It seems that many have been confused and made them think that the 1st Krajina Corps is under the authority of the regional government, which is an utterly wrong conclusion. The 1st Krajina Corps, like all armed establishments of the Serbian people, are under the direct command of the main staff and the relationship between the government and the army and the subordination therein are well defined pursuant to the law on the army. Hence nobody has the right to think that their authority is limitless and to act contrary to the constitution and conclusions that have been passed. I'm just wondering, in light of that, and based upon your experience, if you are aware and were aware that local civilian authorities have absolutely no control over the army, that the army operates under the direction of the main staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even if he tells you yes, Mr. Ackerman, where do we stand? Is he the one who is going to decide on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour. Absolutely correct. I'll go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go to 11 August of 1992, and this is a page that you looked at yesterday, when Ms. Korner was questioning you. It's page L0034477. And it's that story about Celinac, where it says Muslims are allowed to move around for not more than four hours a day. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you just throw into there your own comment that "The best illustration of the atmosphere in this town is the fact that for a long time their political leader was the former president of the municipality, Radoslav Brdjanin." You put that in there yourself, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that exactly but if that's what it says there, then that's what I wrote down. Nobody else had any contact with that diary except myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that Mr. Brdjanin left Celinac in May of 1992 and didn't hold any position of authority there after May of 1992? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So suggesting on 11 August of 1992 that Mr. Brdjanin had something to do with Muslims not being allowed to move around for more than four hours a day was just a gratuitous attack on Mr. Brdjanin on your part, wasn't it, without foundation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Korner --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says the witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- everything that's been going on since Mr. Brdjanin left Celinac and I think has direct consequences on what he organised over there, I believe, and I cannot say decisively but considering his behaviour in Banja Luka, where he had just arrived, I can imagine what it was like in a place where he felt he was the boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's too bad you didn't inquire, because you would have learned that nothing bad was happening in Celinac while Mr. Brdjanin was president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's not have a speech, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Ms. Korner. Point taken, I hope, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk very briefly, sir, about the SOS and the SOS in Banja Luka so we are going to go back now to 3 April, 1992. And I think you will remember on that date, you talked about your phone ringing at 5.00 in the morning and receiving a call from someone who told you there were blockades around the city.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And those blockades were manned by armed individuals who basically took over Banja Luka and made certain demands of the local authorities, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in fact, on page L0051703, I think you referred to them as peasants and criminals, if I have the right page number. Somewhere you referred to them as peasants and criminals. Do you remember that reference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
