utterances.text: I recall that well. I don't know whether you have the exact page number but these are my words and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually the page number was 1704, about two-thirds of the way down. "People born in Banja Luka have lived to see the day when peasants and criminals ID and harass them." That was what you actually wrote, I think. This group that took over the town --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They demanded the creation of a Crisis Staff with whom they could negotiate their demands, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group was organised and armed by the SDS. In order to play that game so to speak, they had a number of requests, this group, to create -- to establish the Crisis Staff and so on. After this was done, this group said that they had ten paragraphs or something, and the Crisis Staff that was established supposedly afterwards responded to them and they fulfilled 11 of them. It was a game, like they asked for ten things and the Crisis Staff fulfilled 11. So they were so -- if they were such criminals that if you had put it all together these people who were on barricades, they would have had 1500 years of prison together. Who gave them the weapons? All this had to be organised. After they became very strong, SDS had to kill them off. For instance, the elimination of Mandic and the others in the Mejdan station and then it went on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You got to make your speech. Now, do you remember the question that I asked you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't I answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. The question was -- Mr. Ackerman asked you whether you know that they demanded the creation of a Crisis Staff with whom or with which they could negotiate their demands. Do you recall that they demanded the creation of a Crisis Staff? Answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recall that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Your next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall that they demanded that war profiteers be arrested and their activities and names be made public?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, why ask him if he recalls it? It's all recorded in his diary. That just takes longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right -- is it recorded in his diary, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move ahead. I think the objection is sustained. That would be part of your submissions later on, I suppose, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the things that they were trying to accomplish was they wanted managers dismissed in all public companies who conducted an anti-Serb policy, and the Crisis Staff response to that was to appoint a committee to deal with that demand. That committee consisted of three persons, Brdjanin, Milinkovic, and Mitrakovic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are getting back to the same thing. All of this is in the diary, word for word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest, Mr. Ackerman, go straight to the relevant part in the diary, because Ms. Korner is absolutely right here, refer the witness to that part and then put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. You were asking him whether he recalls having entered this in his diary. Just go straight to the page and tell him, In your diary on this -- the entry for this particular date, this is what you state. And then go straight to the question that you want to put to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the page -- that page is 0 -- L0051708. At the moment, Your -- Mr. Ackerman -- I'm sorry I'm sitting down. Mr. Ackerman is doing what Your Honour is complaining about that I used to do until I was stopped and just reading the document. What's the actual question? All of this is recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Go straight to the question that you want to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in connection with this task that had been handed to Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Milinkovic, and Mr. Mitrakovic regarding the staff levelling demands made by the SOS, at one point you recorded in your diary, did you not, and it was dealing with a press conference - and I'm on now 5 April of 1992 - a press conference at where Mr. Brdjanin was being asked questions about the staff levelling. He refers to the enterprise Metal. Can you tell us what the enterprise Metal was involved in in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's page L0034674.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. All right. Okay. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What it was involved in, the Metal company, export-import. That's -- that's what they did, the company

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was it's business. Import and export of what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe both. Now, what exactly they did, I don't see why I, as a common citizen, would have been supposed to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can just say you don't know then. That's fine with me. Mr. Brdjanin indicated, did he not, that both the director general and the director were Muslims and that at least -- that a Serb would have to replace one of those two. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know that he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we talked a little bit when you first started your testimony in this case about the proposition that in creating this diary, you came at that process as the person who you were, with all of the biases that you might have personally, and I think you told me that you agreed with that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I was biased? Is that what you're aiming at? I was not biased.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to refer to an entry in your diary very early, 16 January, 1992, and you're speaking there about -- it's page L0034489. You're speaking there about an individual by the name of Borisav Jovic, who I believe at the time was a member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The witness is looking for it but wasn't one of the ones on the list, so he hasn't got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What does -- Mr. Ackerman, what does the witness need to be read to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to read the part to him, Your Honour, beginning with "for Jovic," which is about halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me read it out to him myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, in this entry which goes back to the 16th of January of 1992, you say something about a certain Borisav Jovic giving an interview to the Tanjug, and I'm going to read out to you a part from this paragraph: "For Jovic, the report of the arbitration commission of the conference on Yugoslavia was completely unacceptable, since, as he said, it failed to respect the every nation's right to self-determination and hence transformed the Serbian people in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina from a state forming and constituent nation into a national minority." Do I stop there, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember this entry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, do I remember the entry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your question, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it that you would accept that the Croatian people should be seen as a state-forming people, do you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course. Where do you mean exactly? In Bosnia-Herzegovina or in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Anywhere.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes, I believe they should be viewed as state-forming, same as the Serbs and the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when Mr. Jovic says that the Serbian people in BH and Croatia are being denied that right to self-determination as a state-forming people, what you say one sentence later is: "His spouting of rubbish is just one more proof that this political clown is incapable of grasping reality." So what you're saying is what he's saying about the Serbs being a state-forming people is rubbish. Now, if that's rubbish, why isn't it rubbish that the Croats are too? Or doesn't that just display your bias?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no bias involved. If you think through it again, you will see that Jovic did say that, but for God's sake, no one was trying to turn the Serb people into a minority. What was he basing his statement on, that the Serbs had become a minority anywhere? How in the world should they have been a minority in Bosnia-Herzegovina if they were the most numerous group, as they said? Those were just stories. This was just paving the way for the evil that was coming our way, the dark clouds over our heads, the dark clouds over Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those were just games.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On 16 April, 1992, page L0054897, this is after the creation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina you make this observation: "Today is particularly marked by one absolutely unbelievable move by the Serbian Republic of BH Presidency and government. Today, this parastate requested international recognition. Here are these news that absolutely shocked much of the population of this republic." And then you quote the news item where the Serbian Republic of BH had requested recognition. Now, you had absolutely no shock whatsoever that I can recall about the Bosnian government requesting recognition, internationally, but you seem to be just totally, absolutely shocked that the Serbian republic would request international recognition. Does that not display a bias on your part against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true. There was no bias on my part. Bosnia and Herzegovina was a state, same as Croatia, same as Serbia. But for Republika Srpska, Mr. Ackerman, I can state even here where I'm sitting now that I'm sitting on my own ground and proclaim a republic. I would have the same right as Republika Srpska back then. What exactly does that mean to be on one's own ground? Yes, I was shocked, yes it was a parastate and it still is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have -- you have and you had at the time, some kind of a particular hate or dislike for Mr. Brdjanin, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, well, no, that's simply not true. Simply not true, Mr. Ackerman. Why would I?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's take a look. 27 February of 1992, L0054276, reference to Brdjanin. No wonder that Brdjanin behaved like that. He is after all just a redneck from Celinac. You said that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. I still stand by that, but that doesn't mean I hate him, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On -- well, you certainly don't show much respect. On 3 April, 1992, L0051709, I think I may have the wrong date. No, I don't. You mention four people, five people, Brdjanin, Mitrakovic, Radic, Vukic and Stevandic, as the entire team of fiercest Banja Luka Falcons. Again that's your choice of words, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did describe them as falcons, yes, falcons, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On 5 May, 1992, 03036111, you refer to Mr. Brdjanin as the mastermind behind all this madness. On 7 May, 1992, L0034454, you refer to Mr. Brdjanin as an incompetent politician.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, if I may, with the Court's permission, I may have had my personal opinion on Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because you haven't been asked a question as yet. So let's get on with the question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to refer to a series of what he said, Your Honour, and then ask him one general question about them all. That's what I'm in the process of doing?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, they are all in the diary. If Mr. Ackerman wants to give the page references to all the references to Brdjanin, fine. But I'm anxious to give him an opportunity to re-examine. And just reading the whole -- all the references to Mr. Brdjanin, then asking the question I think is unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are almost finished, Ms. Korner, if I read Mr. Ackerman well. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I told Ms. Korner I would finish by the next break, and I will, quite easily. She'll have plenty of opportunity to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would have been much easier had you collected them on one piece of paper and read these descriptive expressions or, descriptions of Mr. Brdjanin in the diary and then put the question. It would have been much easier. You wouldn't have had to stay referring to the pages and read from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only doing that in fairness to the witness, telling him the date and the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On 25 August of 1992, sir, at page 110057708, you refer to Brdjanin along with Kupresanin, Vukic and Radic as quote, nationalistic scumbags in crime up to their necks. On 4 October, 1992, you say you're referring to a 29 November interview which could not be.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to -- I have to get that actual -- if it's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are you looking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm having trouble finding the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are you looking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe we could be of help, either Ms. Gustin or myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's -- the reference I have in my notes is it's 4 October but it isn't in the 4 October materials here. It's a reference where Mr. Brdjanin is quoted in an interview as saying that the number of Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka has increased. I found it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The page -- it's actually December -- 4 December of 1992 and the page is L0057015. You're referring to an interview given by Mr. Brdjanin entitled "Vipers in the fold." On November 29th of this year. And what Mr. Brdjanin is saying, that if the UNPROFOR forces and the Canadian Battalion located in Banja Luka would mostly be engaged in spying. What you said about Mr. Brdjanin at that point was this: "This filthy little bastard, who as he claims represents the interests of the Serbian people, is the most shameful phenomenon in the history since the homo sapiens has appeared in this land. Any person who possesses even the least sense of honour and decency would be embarrassed by so many shameless lies and lack of scruples. The bastard obviously has never even heard of a category called shame." Now, sir, with that kind of an attitude, I suggest to you that there is no chance that this Chamber could rely on whatever it is you have to say about Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not a proper question. That's a comment and a speech he can make to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained, rephrase your question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That quote, sir, indicates what I suggested to you earlier, that you come here with a complete bias against Mr. Brdjanin, prepared to say anything that you can to hurt him, and I suggest to you that's confirmed by your earlier testimony today where you said something to the effect that he might be seriously damaged by the testimony you give here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What, pray I ask, is the question? Is the question does he have a bias, because if so he ought to be entitled to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that the question is, do you have a bias against Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not particularly fond of Mr. Brdjanin. I never was. That's true. But if any, even the smallest imprecision can be pointed out to me on my part, something that I may have quoted mistakenly, I quoted his statements from TV, radio, newspapers, if you can point out a single, however minute imprecision, something that I'm insinuating to the cost of Mr. Brdjanin, I am prepared to swear another oath and then if that is proven, I can replace him as the accused. I would never insinuate anything that he didn't actually say in order to harm him, if that's what you're aiming at, Mr. Ackerman. You are insinuating that I have a pro-Croatian bias. (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, so can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to stop his answer either, but let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have any questions because I'll tailor my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you may have imagined there are a few questions from Judge Janu, there is just one question from myself which is a very short, straightforward one, and to my understanding, no questions from Judge Taya. So probably we will require between us five minutes, six,.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Seven Minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Six, seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it you don't have a re-examination, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I made that so clear, didn't I, Your Honour? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me explain to the witness what this is all about. Re-examination is a procedure that we follow after the cross-examination, if a request is made for that, and the Prosecution would like to put some questions to you arising from what you stated in the course of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'd like you -- I'm not sure you got, actually, this date. The 5th of March, because you were asked some questions about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is at the LiveNote page 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, yesterday's LiveNote, page 77. He was asked some questions about the 5th of March entries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can deal with this, if the English goes up on -- thank you, Ms. Gustin. This is -- the entry I want to ask you about is at page, in the translation, L0054475. And it's the part where you refer to Stojan Zupljanin talking about the security situation in the Autonomous Region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe -- maybe I'll be proven wrong, but I don't think so. I believe the only thing I referred to from 5 March was the -- that little quote from the diary of Thomas Mann. I don't think that opens up the entire diary of 5 March for re-examination. I think this is beyond the scope of what I covered in cross. Unless I'm shown otherwise, I think that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have to check that before I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's it, that's absolutely right, Your Honour. I'm going to use some of the entries that Mr. Ackerman referred to for his purposes to deal with other entries for my purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I suggest that's totally inappropriate. This wasn't something that was raised on cross for the -- that she can now just because I mentioned 5 March, I don't think she can now question about all diary entries from 5 March. That doesn't open that door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends what the question is. I haven't heard the question as yet, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, but I only referred to the quote from Thomas Mann, and she's over dealing with Stojan Zupljanin on the fifth page of that which has nothing to do with the Thomas Mann quotes. It's brand new material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your question, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The entry refers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I need to find the entry, can you give me the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's 0054475, and it's up on the screen now and you'll see it starts with Stojan Zupljanin, and then there is a comment thereafter. He's referring to Ustasha saboteurs. How could it be possible, says the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is it? I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he goes on to say, how could it be possible with the invincible Banja Luka Corps and a mass troops in a variety of uniforms. Now, Your Honour, I absolutely accept it has nothing to do with the part that Mr. Ackerman referred to, but he's opened the door to an entry. He's picked on something that assists his case in that particular entry. I want to re-examine on another part of that entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In relation to what he was asking yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In relation to -- no, not in relation to the Thomas Mann quote, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm completely unmoved by the Thomas Mann quote. If Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The question, sir, you talk about the Banja Luka Corps there. You were a citizen of Banja Luka. How evident was the corps, the soldiers of the corps, in the streets of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no reason that couldn't have been asked during direct. I certainly didn't ask anything on cross that would justify that question on re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't agree with you. You did. The Banja Luka Corps came up in the course of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She's basing this on my question about this day, the 5 March of 1992. Not on something I questioned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She is picking an extract from -- an excerpt from the entry of 5th March dealing with the Banja Luka Corps, or dealing with what someone supposedly said about the Banja Luka Corps, and she is putting a question that does indeed relate to a part of your cross-examination. So I'm going to allow it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, can you just tell me, as a citizen then of Banja Luka, how evident was the presence of the 5th Corps in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was vast. There were many armed men in olive drab and camouflage uniforms and there was shooting in the sky, non-stop. It was dangerous. There were drunken individuals who had come from the reserve forces and so on. What I particularly recall is one detail, in the evening, there were so many, many -- so much shooting that some birds that were flying, they were -- a lot of them were killed because of the firing up in the air.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you. Now, sir, can we move next to the 5th of May, please, about which you were asked today? Now, you were asked, and you were asked a number of questions about, at the end of your examination, cross-examination, about Mr. Brdjanin and your comments, and you were asked about this interview here and it was put to you that he was effectively not asking -- he was saying that peace, I think, or words to that effect, I can't remember the quote. Can you turn to the first part of that entry for the 5th of May? You describe Brdjanin, this was a quote that wasn't put to you by Mr. Ackerman, I don't think, that Mr. -- "that Brdjanin only wants one thing, he will not give up power at any cost. For the first time a Brdjanin has the chance to enter into history and for the first time he can do anything he wants." Sir, before Mr. Brdjanin achieved power in -- in Banja Luka, did you know anything about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I didn't have a clue. I found out from some people when he arrived, from some people who had worked with him in a company, specifically it was from Milovan Smolic who had worked with him, I found out some details but until then I hadn't heard anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. This is relatively early on in 1992, May. What led to you write then: "He only wants one thing. He will not give up power at any cost. He has a chance to enter into history and do anything he wants." What was it that led you to write that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the only possible conclusion. This person didn't have a -- didn't need a mirror because he had his own TV, he had his own radio. He was there all the time. He practically needed a sofa bed to sleep there. And in all the other media, in Glas and others, every now and then, he would appear, and that's what made me write this. I saw him. I read what he said. I heard what he said. Only a retard wouldn't make -- wouldn't draw this conclusion and wouldn't see the truth of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you move next to the 5th of May, about which you were asked as well? This was another press conference given by Brdjanin, and this is at page L0055644.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 6th of May, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. We've seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, Mr. Ackerman asked questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say there a press conference was held today in Banja Luka where the ARK war staff president, Radoslav Brdjanin, informed the journalists of the most recent decisions made by the staff. And part of that was put to you. These decisions, he said, must be implemented without objections in all 38 ARK municipalities. As far as you were concerned, did you hear him say that or did you read that in the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is what it says here, I just have to see whether this is something I heard or this is something I read in the newspaper. I can't recall. After all it's been quite a few years and you can ask Mr. Brdjanin whether I had added anything or taken something out. If that's what it says here, then it's certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hold it. Try to answer the question and only the question, please. I mean it's -- the question was -- Ms. Korner very rightly put to you a very important question. Are you reporting what you read in a paper here or is this a reporting of a meeting which you yourself attended? And your answer is you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think in fact, Your Honour, earlier -- if one goes back --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a press conference, so if this was carried -- if this was written on that date then it must have been carried by Banja Luka Radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you move now, please, to the 17th of May? Because you were asked about the SOS and you talked -- or you were asked a question and you talked about the showdown between the SOS and the authorities. This is at page L0055598. And it's right at the beginning. You record Radio Banja Luka news, and you say a insolent attack was launched on the police station in the Mejdan local commune in Banja Luka at midnight last night, but was swiftly suppressed. And then there are -- I'm not going to take you through them, but there are further entries about what happened. Is that what you were talking about, the showdown, when the attack on the police station took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right. Exactly that, precisely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, can I ask you to go, please, to the 29th of May, at page L0058435, because you were asked about that in connection with the Crisis Staff saying that Muslims and Croats should be allowed to move out of the Krajina as opposed to being forced to move out. And could you go from there, please, because you quote a lot of the other people, including Mr. Ilic and Dr. Vukic, on this particular topic, and could you go to the part -- this is on page L0058438, where you -- I think it's your comment, and perhaps you can confirm this. The paragraph starts: "Over 1.000 Muslims have been taken prisoner on the battle fields. The Serbian army treats them humanely and tries to help them move to those territories where they want to live. Nothing will happen to any Muslim or Croat."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to bring it -- you passed it already, just a few lines. Stop, stop, stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Nothing will happen to any -- I think -- I'm sorry, this may be Mr. Ilic, if you look at the previous page, "And therefore there is no reason for them to flee other Banja Luka or Bosanska Krajina." And then you make a comment about Mr. Vukic or Dr. Vukic. And talks about the fact that they have been transferred to Omarska. I'm sorry, Your Honour, in fact this is an error. I mean it's actually not a question at all. So I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 10th of June, please. Now, your attention was drawn, please, and this is at page L0055807, where the War Presidency of the Municipal Assembly, in fact, not of the regional assembly, approved the request of the Banja Luka Mufti Halilovic, changing the curfew, and then there is a long list of those instructions. Can you go now, please, in your diary to the part where you deal with the form? And it's on our page L0055810. I think the suggestion was that there was the municipal Crisis Staff or War Presidency acceding to a request by a Muslim. However, if you look at what you said about it, you said, and this is -- yes, the top of the page, "That the place where this announcement was published was to say, the least, inappropriate. Below it are five obituaries of people who lost their lives in this unfortunate war and altogether this seems to me more as another challenge to local extremists to persecute the Muslim population than and expression --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Ms. Korner slow down when reading, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "-- more than an expression and gesture of goodwill. At this time, where not a single positive word about Muslims can be read or heard in the local media, and when they are all Islamic fundamentalists, extremists or fanatics, this is just pouring oil on the fire," and so on. Is that something that you in your judgement felt was done deliberately, i.e., the placing of this announcement above the obituaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that as a provocation, as a simple provocation. If, for instance, some stupid goods are being advertised, sugar or something, at a more appropriate place, then it can only be understood as a provocation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour, I think two things. Number 1, Ms. Korner is doing what she criticised me for and that's just reading the diary to you. And number 2, I think in all fairness if she is going to do that, the last sentence of that paragraph needs to be read because it goes directly to the question that was asked of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, I'm quite happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me read it as well, Ms. Korner. Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In any case, if this was not intentionally, then very thoughtlessly done and will bring more harm than benefit to relations between these two until recent brotherly peoples who are moving increasingly further away from each other, at least in Bosnia." Can we move finally to three entries that you were referred to in July or some entries? Yes. 15th of July, please. You were referred to parts relating to the War Presidency, I think, and the argument with Glas. I just want to -- yes. And I think this also relates to the suggestion that Mr. Brdjanin was not trying to force people to leave and the whole -- the Bosnian Serbs are not trying to force people to leave Banja Luka. Can you turn to page -- the page that begins -- well, it's a paragraph that begins at page L0048332, "During the past 24 hours a total of ten crimes have been reported in Banja Luka." But I want you to go to what's the part that begins, "Day in, day out, the area is being ethnically cleansed by force," which is L0048333. You say, "Day in, day out, the area is being ethnically cleansed by force and thousands of people are trying to leave the territory of the Krajina in an attempt to save the only thing that remains to be saved. The local media still present the huge Muslim and Croat migrations and abandonment of their centuries old homes as the acts of generosity on the part of the usurpers of power. An impression is being created that Catholic churches and mosques are destroyed by Croats and Muslims respectively. The fact that the Muslims and Croats are moving out is accounted for, believe it or not, by the fact that both Croats and Muslims fear the extremists in their own respective ranks who will not let them live in love and peace with their Serbian neighbours."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman? You're objecting to the reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, she objected to me doing it and you sustained her objection and I stopped and skipped a whole bunch of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I sustain your objection. So let's move with the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions today about the reason why you and others left. That is what you wrote in 1992. Is that your opinion today or have you changed that opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions today about people leaving voluntarily, like yourself. In 1992, you wrote the paragraph that we've just read, namely that the area was being ethnically cleansed by force. Is that your opinion today or have you altered your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't changed my opinion, not at all, not in the least.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I think that will do because the last question I can deal with in argument. Sir, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Judge Janu has some questions for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, at the beginning of your testimony, you told us that ethnicity wasn't an important factor in your lives, and you gave the example that you didn't know the ethnicity of half of your friends and they didn't know -- many of them didn't ask -- didn't know yours. Could you please assist the Chamber in this problem? How was it possible that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there still were villages who were ethnically clean, who were Muslims or Serbs or Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a very hard question to answer, but I can try. In principle, yes, there were villages that were ethnically clean, but there were very few villages where you had Muslims and Serbs together. That was very difficult to find in Bosnia. But it wasn't a rare occurrence that there were villages with Croats and Muslims mixed. I find it very difficult, and I ask myself often how did this occur? Why did this happen? And why did this occur? We lived for centuries together. Urban part is a different story in Bosnia. In Bosnia, there is a big difference between the rural and the urban part. The rural part is one responsible for everything that happened because it's the rural population that believed all those stories they were being told, and that's when we started to sort of fight for some kind of security, that's when all security eluded us and that's when everything occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Can you tell me what does it mean, calling Mr. Brdjanin a redneck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a redneck, when we say that in Bosnia, when we use the expression, we don't mean the farmers, the people working the land, that's not what we have in mind. When we call someone a redneck, that's usually pejorative. It's derogatory. I've got to tell you that. The expression is used in this case because certainly in town -- well in Bosnia, you know there is a proverb which says the wild ones came along and chased away the tame ones. Those people came, all of a sudden, and started imposing their feral habits and customs on us so these were the people we referred to as rednecks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: You said, and we were discussing Mr. Ackerman touched that point, that in your diary, there is an entry that Mr. Brdjanin was a core member of the Crisis Staff and you also said that he had unlimited access to the media and television. My question is: Did you ever hear Mr. Brdjanin saying that he is about to leave Crisis Staff because he's always voting against the majority? That the decisions are adopted against his will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember having heard anything like that. I can't say that I didn't, but I don't remember. If I've heard anything like that, I would have written it down in my diary and it must be there in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: My next question is: Can you tell us, please, why did you consider former President Tudjman regime fatal for Croatia? Why? 20

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vital? I'm not sure what you mean but probably you're asking me why I criticised President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Fatal, why did you consider former President Tudjman's regime to be fatal for Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because he did everything he could against Bosnia and by dint of that he was working against Croatia too. Tudjman was no better than Milosevic. He was just a smaller player in a manner of speaking. Milosevic was the more intelligent one. I'm quite convinced. Tudjman would speak openly about things that Milosevic tended to conceal or speak less openly about. He'd be carrying the branch of peace and, well, the international community respected him in a way, whereas the other one had no brains to even conceal his intention to destroy Bosnia and tear it to pieces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question is: Could you please estimate the role of propaganda in the conflict in your municipality and in Bosnia-Herzegovina maybe some sort of summary, if you would be so kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion, and my deepest conviction, that all those who were killed in the actual war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, had been killed even before they were physically killed by the electronic media. I think that's the briefest form in which I can put this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, to butt in like this, Judge Janu, but I haven't understood your answer. Perhaps if you could repeat it, you were asked by Judge Janu -- one moment -- "Could you please estimate the role of propaganda in the conflict in your municipality and the BH, maybe some sort of summary, if you would be so kind?" And you said that, "It is your deepest conviction that all those who were killed in the actual war in Bosnia and Herzegovina had been killed even before they were physically killed, by the electronic media. I think this is the briefest form in which I can put this. But I think it calls also for an explanation. In other words, are you saying that the mass media was mobilised in order to procure the genocide of these people or not? The killing of these people or not? The physical elimination of these people or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The media were not calling for genocide but the media were creating an atmosphere which led to the misfortune that occurred. It's the media's fault most of all. Who would have heard Mr. Brdjanin speaking had it not been for Radio Banja Luka, TV Banja Luka, TV Pale? If the local newspapers hadn't been there? It was the media that paved the way. They paved the way for what eventually happened to our deepest regret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have one real question but I'm going to divide it into parts. You mentioned yesterday, and you also mentioned it today as well, or you referred to Brdjanin, Kupresanin, Vukic and Radic as the four horsemen of the apocalypse. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In your opinion, having lived those days, and even bothered to write a diary, who was the most powerful amongst those four horsemen of the apocalypse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very difficult call. It's very difficult to estimate. Vukic was the most primitive one. Brdjanin was the most aggressive one. Radic was the vilest and Kupresanin was an ambiguous personality. You couldn't really tell what he was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My question relates to power. At the end of the day, if you squeezed all the juice out of --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was the most powerful? Who wielded the power, in reality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, who wielded the power, who was the driving force? Difficult to say really. Most of the fatal decisions, at least the way it seemed, were taken by Brdjanin. I'm not sure if that was only an outward representation of his power and his desire to be in the forefront. It's very difficult for me to say. Maybe there was someone else behind all of them, without me knowing. Maybe it was something we didn't know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You used the term apocalypse as a context in which you qualify or described these four persons. Apocalypse has a connotation of a disaster, an utter, complete disaster, a cataclysm. Would you consider the four horsemen of the apocalypse that you say you lived equally responsible or would you say that any one of them is more responsible than the others? In which case I would like to know who.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I wouldn't single out any which one of them because it's very difficult for me to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Next question. Who appeared in the media or who figured in the media most out of the four?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without the shadow of a doubt, Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And my penultimate question: In the events that took place there, is there any particular area of activity which you describe as being directed against the Muslims and/or the Croats? Is there such an area that that you would hold Brdjanin responsible for more than the other three?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at the head of the staff which was in charge of the ethnic levelling, a staff which had the power to dismiss anti-Serbian persons. Your Honours, you too would be dismissed at their hands because in their eyes you would have been anti-Serbian. Their policy was if you're not with us, you're against us. Why would I have supported someone there only in order to be viewed as a constructive person? I think he was the one who was in charge of dismissing managers, dismissing people from their jobs. A little while ago, we talked about two managers who were Muslims. Why wouldn't they be Muslims and managers if they are competent people? Why would we not have three managers who are Serbs, if they are fully qualified to do their job? That's what it's about. I think that was the biggest sin that Radoslav Brdjanin committed. Whether he called the shots alone made these decisions alone, I don't know. It's not for me to say but he was the one who informed the public about these decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My last, very last, question to you but I have to clear up something with Judge Taya, I think I better clear that up first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At a certain point during your testimony, and while you were answering one of my questions, you said that the most vital or fatal decisions, at least the way it seemed to you, were taken by Brdjanin. What motivates you, on what grounds do you reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had the impression because all the most fatal things that were communicated through the media, radio, TV or papers by Mr. Brdjanin to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. My very last question and then you can leave. A few minutes ago, you drew more or less a comparison between Milosevic and Tudjman and you said that Tudjman was not such a big player as Milosevic was. How big a player was Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the context of Republika Srpska? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the context of the ARK. The Autonomous Region of Krajina. And Republika Srpska. Take it as you like.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, he was certainly quite a big player. As for Republika Srpska, I think even there he was near the top, near the very top. It's difficult for me to say but I think he was near the top. After all, he was a man who dared to even oppose Karadzic himself sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir, for having come over to give evidence in this trial against Radoslav Brdjanin. I thank you not only on my behalf but on behalf of Judge Janu from the Czech Republic and Judge Taya from Japan sitting together with me in this trial as judges. You will receive all the assistance you require by the staff of this Tribunal to enable to you return to your country. On behalf of everyone present here I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honours. Good luck.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just raise tomorrow? That is that we have set aside two days for the next witness. I'd like to know, please, if I can in advance, how long Your Honours will give me for examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who will be cross-examining the witness? Roughly? How much time do you require.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A day or less, that's my guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can have the whole of tomorrow for sure and then Mr. Ackerman would be in a better position to say whether he requires a full day or less. I take it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just check as well, did we -- I thought I had made the diary an exhibit but I can't be 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it was made -- I better not comment on that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If can I formally apply -- I think I did, but can I formally apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 2326. And, Your Honour, finally then can I mention the binders for Celinac, Bosanska Krupa and Kotor Varos? I'm told that none have been admitted, the documents therein, may I ask that they are formally admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will decide that tomorrow because I have to check about any objections that Mr. Ackerman may have raised. I think we did deal with the Celinac ones for sure here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Objections were raised, no they weren't actually I don't think any objections have been raised with Celinac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With Celinac I think there was, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly not to Krupa yet and not to Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't remember, Ms. Korner, I think I need to check that with my staff first and then we will take a decision tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I have objections to Celinac and Krupa filed and I have not yet filed Kotor Varos but will. I just haven't gotten there yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I wish to thank you once more the interpreters and the technicians and all the other remaining staff for overstaying with us for more than five minutes. I thank you and I really appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
